## ON OPTICS OR PERSPECTIVE

are [the opinions on the nature of sight]. For Plato believes that sight is produced according to clarity, namely by a light flowing from the eyes toward an external air, and by the light from bodies being reflected back to meet it; that which is in the medium of the air is easily poured forth and converted, extended alongside the fire-formed power of sight. Galen agrees with Plato; but Hipparchus says that rays extended from the eyes to bodies touch them as if by a certain palpitation, rendering their perception to the sight. The Epicureans, however, affirm that the likenesses of those things which appear force themselves upon the eyes. Aristotle, on the other hand, believes that the likenesses are not indeed bodies, but that they arrive from visible things to the sight through an alteration of the air which is in the circuit, according to its quality. Porphyry, however, considers neither rays, nor likenesses, nor anything else to be the cause of seeing; but rather that the soul itself, knowing itself to be visible, and being one in all things, knows itself in all things that exist. But the geometers and opticians, approaching Hipparchus in a certain way, subscribe to certain cones formed from the coincidence of rays which are emitted through the eyes: from which the sight comprehends many visible things at once, but those most clearly where the rays have coincided. But indeed, Alchindus <note>referring to Al-Kindi, the 9th-century Arab polymath who wrote extensively on optics</note> teaches something entirely different regarding aspects, and it seems to Augustine that the power of the soul in the eye achieves something that has not yet been investigated by those studious of wisdom. This science, therefore, contributes greatly to the apprehension of the variety, distance, magnitude, and motion of celestial bodies, as well as their reflections and refractions; it also serves architecture in the measuring of buildings. It is, however, closest to the art of painting, and confers the greatest ornament to the manufacture of mirrors, so that without it these arts cannot be perfected. For it shows by what reason we should not fashion things as distorted or misshapen in the images that are seen on account of intervals and altitudes.

<summary>This page explores various historical and philosophical theories regarding the nature of vision, contrasting the perspectives of Plato, Galen, Hipparchus, the Epicureans, Aristotle, Porphyry, and Al-Kindi, while noting the practical applications of optics in architecture, painting, and mirror-making.</summary>
